chapter_text:
CHAPTER 10 — CLIMATE

Introduction

Weather and CLIMATE are not the same. WEATHER is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere — temperature, humidity, rain, wind — at a particular place and time. CLIMATE is the AVERAGE pattern of weather over a long period (typically 30 years or more) for a region. India's climate is broadly described as the TROPICAL MONSOON type, but enormous regional variation exists — the country contains everything from the wettest place on earth (Mawsynram, Meghalaya) to one of its driest (the Thar Desert), from snow-bound Ladakh to the equatorial humidity of the southern islands.

10.1 FACTORS AFFECTING INDIAN CLIMATE

Six major factors shape India's climate:

(1) LATITUDE — the Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India. The southern half is TROPICAL; the northern half is SUB-TROPICAL. This means temperatures stay relatively high all year in the south, but show greater seasonal variation in the north.

(2) ALTITUDE — temperature falls with altitude (~6.5 °C per 1000 m on average). Hence the Himalayas have much cooler climates than the plains at the same latitude; this is why people retreat to hill stations in summer.

(3) PRESSURE AND WINDS — the seasonal reversal of winds (the monsoon) is the most distinctive feature of Indian climate. In summer, low pressure over the heated landmass draws moist winds from the sea; in winter, high pressure over land sends dry winds out to sea.

(4) DISTANCE FROM THE SEA — coastal areas have moderate, EQUABLE climates (small annual temperature range); interior areas have CONTINENTAL climates (large daily and annual temperature ranges). Mumbai and Pune are at similar latitudes but Pune's range is much larger.

(5) RELIEF (mountain barriers) — the Himalayas block cold northern winds; the Western Ghats force the monsoon to release rain over the west coast. Such orographic effects make local climates strikingly different.

(6) OCEAN CURRENTS — warm currents (e.g. North Equatorial) raise coastal temperatures and humidity; cold currents have the opposite effect.

10.2 THE INDIAN MONSOON

The word MONSOON comes from the Arabic 'mausim' meaning 'season'. Indian agriculture, water supply, electricity and even economic growth depend on the monsoon. The simple explanation:

 - In SUMMER (April-June) the Indian landmass heats up dramatically; air over the land rises, creating low atmospheric pressure. The Indian Ocean, slower to warm, remains relatively cool with higher pressure. Air therefore flows from sea to land — moisture-laden SOUTH-WEST winds blow from the Indian Ocean over the Indian subcontinent. As these winds rise over the Western Ghats or are forced upward by the Himalayas, they cool and release their water as rain. This is the SOUTH-WEST MONSOON (June-September), which gives India over 75% of its annual rainfall.

 - In WINTER (December-February) the land cools faster than the sea, creating high pressure over the land and lower pressure over the sea. Winds therefore reverse — DRY NORTH-EAST winds blow from land to sea. These winds pick up some moisture as they cross the Bay of Bengal and bring winter rains to the Tamil Nadu coast (the NORTH-EAST MONSOON or 'retreating monsoon').

The ARRIVAL of the SW monsoon (called the 'BURST OF MONSOON') around 1 June at Kerala is one of the most-watched events in Indian life. From Kerala the monsoon advances northward and reaches Delhi by about end of June. It retreats southward from September.

10.3 THE FOUR SEASONS

Indian Meteorological Department recognises four seasons:

(1) WINTER (December-February) — Cool, dry. North India: clear skies, cool/cold days, cold nights. Westerly disturbances bring some rain to northern plains and snow to Himalayas. South India: mild, with NE monsoon rains on Tamil Nadu coast.

(2) HOT WEATHER / SUMMER (March-May) — Hot and dry. Temperatures over much of the country rise above 35-40 °C. Loo winds (hot dry westerly) blow across the Northern Plains. Convectional thunderstorms occur (mango showers in Kerala, Kalbaisakhi or norwesters in Bengal).

(3) RAINY SEASON / SOUTH-WEST MONSOON (June-September) — Monsoon advances northward from Kerala. Heavy rains over Western Ghats, north-east India, and northern plains. Causes more than three-fourths of India's rainfall.

(4) RETREATING / POST-MONSOON (October-November) — Monsoon retreats; weather hot, humid (October heat); cyclones may form in the Bay of Bengal hitting Odisha/Andhra. Tamil Nadu gets most of its rainfall from this NE monsoon.

10.4 RAINFALL DISTRIBUTION IN INDIA

Indian rainfall is highly UNEVEN, both seasonally and regionally:
 - VERY HIGH (>250 cm): Western coast, Western Ghats, north-eastern states (Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura). Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya are among the wettest places in the world.
 - MEDIUM HIGH (150-250 cm): Sub-Himalayan region, Odisha, Bengal.
 - MODERATE (75-150 cm): Most of the Northern Plains, Madhya Pradesh, eastern Rajasthan, much of the Deccan.
 - LOW (50-75 cm): Western UP, southern Punjab, central Deccan, Tamil Nadu interior.
 - VERY LOW (<50 cm): Western Rajasthan, Ladakh, parts of Gujarat.

Seasonally, MOST rain (~75%) falls in just FOUR MONTHS (June-September). The remaining months are mostly dry.

10.5 CLIMATIC REGIONS OF INDIA

India is divided into broadly six climatic regions:

(1) TROPICAL RAINY — west coast and Western Ghats; heavy rainfall, warm temperatures all year.
(2) TROPICAL SAVANNA — most of the Peninsular Plateau; clear winter, hot summer, monsoon rainfall.
(3) TROPICAL/SUBTROPICAL STEPPE — semi-arid; central western India.
(4) TROPICAL DESERT — Thar; arid.
(5) HUMID SUBTROPICAL — Northern Plains; hot summer, cool winter, monsoon rains.
(6) MOUNTAIN — Himalayas; cold, variable, snow-covered at high elevations.

SUMMARY

- Weather is short-term and local; climate is long-term and regional.
- India's climate is shaped by latitude, altitude, pressure-and-winds, distance from sea, relief, and ocean currents.
- The monsoon — seasonal reversal of winds — gives India over 75% of its annual rainfall.
- The SW monsoon bursts in Kerala around 1 June and advances north; the NE monsoon brings winter rains to Tamil Nadu.
- IMD recognises four seasons: winter, hot-summer, rainy (SW monsoon), retreating monsoon.
- Rainfall is highly uneven — Mawsynram is among the wettest places on earth, the Thar is desert.

chapter_summary.title: Climate — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Social Science (213) summary for Lesson 10. India's climate is broadly tropical monsoon, but with vast regional variation. The chapter studies the factors that shape Indian climate, the monsoon system that dominates it, the four seasons of the climatic year, the highly uneven distribution of rainfall, and India's six broad climatic regions.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Climate
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Use specific seasonal and regional names where appropriate.

questions.question: Distinguish between weather and climate.
questions.answer: WEATHER is the state of the atmosphere at a place at a particular time, described by temperature, humidity, pressure, wind, cloud and precipitation. It can change from hour to hour. CLIMATE is the average pattern of weather over a long period (typically 30 years or more) for a region. Weather is short-term and local; climate is long-term and regional. Example: a thunderstorm in Delhi today = weather; the fact that Delhi has hot summers and mild winters with most rain in July-August = climate.

questions.question: List the six factors that affect India's climate.
questions.answer: (1) LATITUDE — the Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India; south of it is tropical, north of it sub-tropical. (2) ALTITUDE — temperature falls with elevation; Himalayan regions are cooler than plains at the same latitude. (3) PRESSURE AND WINDS — seasonal reversal of winds (monsoon) is the dominant feature. (4) DISTANCE FROM THE SEA — coastal regions have moderate (equable) climates, interior regions have larger temperature ranges. (5) RELIEF — mountain barriers (Himalayas, Western Ghats) block winds and force them to rise (orographic rainfall). (6) OCEAN CURRENTS — warm and cold currents along the coast modify coastal temperatures and humidity.

questions.question: Explain the mechanism of the south-west monsoon.
questions.answer: In the SUMMER (April-June) the Indian landmass HEATS UP rapidly and reaches very high temperatures. The hot air over the land rises, leaving a region of LOW PRESSURE over north-west India (Thar Desert area, in particular). The Indian Ocean, having a high heat capacity, warms up much more slowly and so retains relatively HIGH PRESSURE. Since wind always flows from high to low pressure, air now FLOWS FROM THE SEA TO THE LAND. These winds, having travelled over the Indian Ocean, are loaded with MOISTURE. As they reach the Indian coast, especially the Western Ghats, the moisture-laden air is forced to RISE; rising air cools, and water vapour CONDENSES into rain. This is the SOUTH-WEST MONSOON — bringing over 75% of India's annual rainfall during June-September.

questions.question: What is the 'burst of monsoon'? When and where does it occur?
questions.answer: The 'BURST OF MONSOON' is the sudden onset of heavy south-west monsoon rains after the relatively dry, hot pre-monsoon period. It is dramatic — temperatures fall, skies darken, heavy rains begin, often within a single day. It TYPICALLY ARRIVES around 1 JUNE on the KERALA coast. From there it advances northward — reaching Mumbai by ~10 June, Kolkata by mid-June, Delhi by end of June, and the entire country by mid-July. The 'burst' is one of the most-watched and culturally significant events of the Indian year — songs, festivals and farming all centre around it.

questions.question: What is the north-east monsoon? Which region depends on it?
questions.answer: In winter (December onwards) the landmass cools rapidly, creating HIGH PRESSURE over land. The Indian Ocean remains warmer (LOW PRESSURE). Winds therefore FLOW FROM LAND TO SEA — dry NORTH-EAST winds blowing out of the Indian subcontinent. As these winds cross the BAY OF BENGAL, they pick up moisture, and when they strike the south-eastern coast they release this moisture as RAIN. This NORTH-EAST MONSOON (October-December) brings winter rains to the TAMIL NADU coast and parts of southern Andhra Pradesh — regions that are in the rain-shadow of the south-west monsoon. Tamil Nadu receives most of its annual rainfall from the NE monsoon.

questions.question: Name the four seasons of the Indian climatic year (as per IMD) and state one feature of each.
questions.answer:
(1) WINTER (Dec-Feb) — cool, dry; westerly disturbances may bring rain to north; NE monsoon gives rain to Tamil Nadu.
(2) HOT WEATHER / SUMMER (Mar-May) — very hot; temperatures cross 40 °C in north and central India; loo winds; thunderstorms (Kalbaisakhi, mango showers).
(3) RAINY SEASON / SW MONSOON (Jun-Sep) — main rainfall season; over 75% of annual rain falls.
(4) RETREATING / POST-MONSOON (Oct-Nov) — monsoon withdraws; humid 'October heat'; cyclones in Bay of Bengal; Tamil Nadu's main rainy season.

questions.question: Why is the rainfall in India so uneven?
questions.answer: Several reasons: (1) The major moisture-bearing winds (south-west monsoon) come from the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal; areas FACING these winds (west coast, north-east) get heavy rain. (2) The WESTERN GHATS block the monsoon's westerly approach — the WESTERN slope gets heavy rain while the EASTERN side falls in a RAIN-SHADOW. (3) The HIMALAYAS force the Bay branch of the monsoon upward, giving heavy rain to north-east India. (4) The THAR DESERT lies parallel to the monsoon winds, which slide over it without much rainfall. (5) Tamil Nadu gets little SW monsoon (it lies parallel to those winds) and depends instead on the NE monsoon. (6) Local topography (mountains, valleys) modifies rainfall over short distances. So rainfall is shaped by the interaction of wind direction with mountain barriers — and India's complex topography creates extreme variation.

questions.question: Why are Mawsynram and Cherrapunji among the wettest places on earth?
questions.answer: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji are both in the Khasi Hills of MEGHALAYA in north-east India. As the south-west monsoon's BAY OF BENGAL branch advances inland from the Bay, it is FUNNELLED INTO the narrow valleys of Meghalaya — surrounded by the Himalayas to the north and the Burmese mountains to the east. The moisture-laden air is forced sharply UPWARD by the Khasi Hills, cooling rapidly and releasing torrential rain. Mawsynram averages about 11 000-12 000 mm of annual rainfall (compared with India's average of ~120 cm = 1200 mm) — almost ten times the national average. Cherrapunji holds historical records of nearly 26 000 mm in a single year.

questions.question: Why is the monsoon so important for India?
questions.answer: The monsoon is the lifeblood of India: (1) AGRICULTURE — over half of cultivated land is rain-fed; the timing and quantity of monsoon rain determine farm output and farmer incomes. (2) WATER SUPPLY — rivers, reservoirs and groundwater all depend on monsoon recharge. (3) HYDROPOWER — depends on monsoon-fed reservoirs. (4) ECONOMY — a good monsoon boosts GDP, rural demand, food prices and inflation. (5) FOOD SECURITY — monsoon failure (drought) can cause food shortages. (6) CULTURE — Indian songs, poetry, religious festivals (Teej, Raksha Bandhan) are tied to the monsoon. The phrase 'every Indian budget is a gamble on the monsoon' captures its central role.

questions.question: Identify the six climatic regions of India and give one example region for each.
questions.answer:
(1) TROPICAL RAINY — heavy rain (>200 cm), warm all year. Example: west coast (Konkan, Malabar) and Western Ghats.
(2) TROPICAL SAVANNA — distinct wet and dry seasons; moderate rainfall (75-150 cm). Example: most of the Deccan Plateau (Karnataka, Maharashtra interior).
(3) TROPICAL / SUBTROPICAL STEPPE — semi-arid; 25-75 cm rainfall. Example: eastern Rajasthan, parts of Haryana.
(4) TROPICAL DESERT — arid; <25 cm rainfall. Example: western Rajasthan (Thar).
(5) HUMID SUBTROPICAL — hot summer, cool winter, monsoon rain. Example: most of the Northern Plains (Punjab, UP, Bihar).
(6) MOUNTAIN climate — cold, snow at high elevations. Example: Himalayan states (J&K, Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal).

How does altitude affect climate? Give an example.
questions.answer: Temperature decreases with ALTITUDE — roughly 6.5 °C per 1000 m. Hence high-altitude places are cooler than low-altitude places at the same latitude. EXAMPLE: Shimla and Chandigarh are at almost the same latitude in north India, but Shimla (~2200 m elevation) is 10-15 °C cooler than Chandigarh (~300 m) at most times of year. This is why Indians built hill stations — Shimla, Mussoorie, Darjeeling, Ooty — at altitude to escape summer plains heat.

questions.question: Why are Mumbai's summer temperatures milder than Delhi's, even though both are at similar latitudes?
questions.answer: Because of DISTANCE FROM THE SEA. Mumbai is on the Arabian Sea coast; Delhi is deep in the continental interior. The sea has a much greater HEAT CAPACITY than land — it warms slowly in summer and cools slowly in winter. So coastal Mumbai gains and loses heat slowly, producing an EQUABLE climate: summer maxima rarely cross 35 °C; winter minima rarely fall below 15 °C. Delhi, by contrast, has a CONTINENTAL climate: summers cross 45 °C; winter nights fall to 4-5 °C. The same logic explains why Chennai is milder than Hyderabad in summer.

questions.question: What are the two branches of the south-west monsoon?
questions.answer:
(1) ARABIAN SEA BRANCH — picks up moisture over the Arabian Sea; strikes the Western Ghats from the west; gives heavy rain to the west coast (Kerala, Konkan, Goa) and crosses to bring rain to the Deccan interior, north India and west.
(2) BAY OF BENGAL BRANCH — picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal; reaches north-east India and the eastern Himalayas; one part is funnelled into the Khasi Hills (giving Mawsynram its huge rainfall); another part flows up the Ganga valley westward, bringing rain to north Indian plains.

questions.question: Describe the four seasons of India in greater detail.
questions.answer:
(1) WINTER (Dec-Feb): Cool, dry. North India sees clear skies and cool/cold days. Westerly disturbances bring rain to north plains and snow to the Himalayas. Tamil Nadu gets NE monsoon rains.

(2) HOT WEATHER (Mar-May): Sun moves north; temperatures rise sharply. Northern Plains see >40 °C; Rajasthan often >45 °C. The 'loo' (hot dry westerly) blows; dust storms; convectional storms (Kalbaisakhi in Bengal, mango showers in Kerala, andhis in Punjab).

(3) RAINY SEASON / SW MONSOON (Jun-Sep): The monsoon bursts on Kerala around 1 June; advances over the entire country by mid-July. Heavy rains over Western Ghats, NE India, Himalayas, Northern Plains. >75% of annual rainfall falls in these four months.

(4) RETREATING / POST-MONSOON (Oct-Nov): The monsoon retreats southward. Skies clear, but humidity remains high — the 'October heat'. Cyclones form in the Bay of Bengal and strike Odisha/Andhra coast. Tamil Nadu enters its rainy season.

questions.question: What are the consequences of uneven and uncertain rainfall in India?
questions.answer:
(1) AGRICULTURE — areas with high, reliable rainfall (Punjab, west coast) have intensive farming and high yields; arid areas (Thar) have pastoral economies. Variable rain means harvest risk for over half of India's farmers (rain-fed agriculture).
(2) FLOODS AND DROUGHTS — concentrated rainfall in just 4 months means floods are common (Bihar, Assam, Bengal) while other months see drought conditions (much of central India).
(3) WATER MANAGEMENT — need for reservoirs, irrigation, groundwater. Areas like Rajasthan rely on canals (Indira Gandhi Canal).
(4) ECONOMIC IMPACT — a poor monsoon hurts GDP, raises food prices, increases farmer distress. The phrase 'every Indian budget is a gamble on the monsoon' captures this.
(5) POPULATION DISTRIBUTION — densely populated where water is reliable (Northern Plains); sparse in deserts and rain-shadow areas.
(6) MIGRATION — drought drives rural-to-urban migration each year.

questions.question: Name the six climatic regions of India.
questions.answer: (1) TROPICAL RAINY — west coast, Western Ghats. (2) TROPICAL SAVANNA — most of Peninsular Plateau. (3) TROPICAL/SUBTROPICAL STEPPE — semi-arid central-western India. (4) TROPICAL DESERT — Thar. (5) HUMID SUBTROPICAL — Northern Plains. (6) MOUNTAIN — Himalayas.

questions.question: Why is the monsoon often called the 'backbone of the Indian economy'?
questions.answer: Because so much of India's economic life depends on it: (1) AGRICULTURE — over 50% of cultivated land is rain-fed; the kharif (summer) crop (rice, jowar, bajra, maize, cotton, sugarcane) depends almost entirely on the SW monsoon. (2) GROUNDWATER and SURFACE WATER recharge depends on monsoon. (3) HYDROPOWER — reservoirs need monsoon inflows; electricity availability fluctuates with rainfall. (4) FOOD PRICES — a poor monsoon raises food prices and inflation across the country. (5) RURAL DEMAND — good monsoons mean farm incomes rise, fueling demand for two-wheelers, FMCG, electronics — boosting GDP. (6) FISCAL POSITION — poor monsoons increase government spending on relief, subsidies. So the monsoon's success or failure ripples through the entire economy — making it the literal backbone.

questions.question: Explain why the Thar Desert is so dry despite being surrounded by relatively wetter regions.
questions.answer: Several reasons: (1) The south-west monsoon winds blow PARALLEL to the Aravalli range (which lies roughly north-east to south-west) rather than perpendicular. So the winds glide ALONGSIDE rather than OVER the Aravallis and are not forced to rise to release moisture as rain. (2) By the time the Arabian Sea branch reaches western Rajasthan, it has largely exhausted its moisture over the Western Ghats. (3) The desert is far INLAND from the Bay of Bengal branch. (4) High SUMMER TEMPERATURES (often >45 °C) cause evaporation to exceed rainfall — moisture that does fall is lost quickly. (5) Some clouds do form but cannot be cooled enough to release rain over the heated desert. Together these factors keep annual rainfall under 150 mm — true desert conditions.

questions.question: How do the Himalayas act as a climatic barrier for India?
questions.answer: In two ways: (1) Northward, they BLOCK the cold dry continental winds from Central Asia — which is why northern India is warmer in winter than countries at similar latitudes like Mongolia or Kazakhstan. (2) Southward, they STOP the south-west monsoon winds; the moisture-laden winds are forced to RISE over the Himalayas, cooling and releasing huge quantities of rain on the southern slopes — Cherrapunji and Mawsynram in the eastern Himalayan foothills are among the rainiest places on earth.

questions.question: Describe the advance and retreat of the Indian monsoon.
questions.answer:
ADVANCE OF SW MONSOON:
 - ~1 June: bursts onto the Kerala coast.
 - By 5-10 June: covers Karnataka, Goa, Andhra coast.
 - By 10-15 June: reaches Mumbai (Maharashtra), parts of MP.
 - By 15 June: covers Bengal, eastern Bihar, north-east India.
 - By 20-25 June: reaches UP, Delhi, Haryana.
 - By 1 July: covers western UP, eastern Rajasthan, Gujarat.
 - By 15 July: covers most of the country including western Rajasthan.

RETREAT (or 'withdrawal') OF SW MONSOON:
 - Mid-September: monsoon begins to retreat from north-west India (Rajasthan, Punjab).
 - End September: withdraws from north India.
 - October: withdraws from central India.
 - November: withdraws from the south.
 - By mid-December: completely withdrawn.

As the SW monsoon retreats from the south, the winds reverse and the NORTH-EAST MONSOON sets in — bringing winter rain to Tamil Nadu, southern Andhra and Kerala in October-December.
